source.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Sequential Recommendation Models: Interpretation and Flexible Control
source.authors: Anton Klenitskiy; Konstantin Polev; Daria Denisova; A. Vasilev; Dmitry Simakov; G. Gusev

record.tranche_reason: The study measures SAE reconstruction error under different L1 penalties and dictionary sizes, bearing narrowly on whether training choices affect the residual's magnitude. It does not analyze residual structure or test the dark-matter claims' other proposed mechanisms.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports reconstruction error and recommendation metrics after replacing a transformer layer's activations with SAE reconstructions. The dictionary-size result is stated in text as reconstruction error remaining stable from 512 to 8192. These measurements do not test linear predictability, per-token error norms or token overlap, comparisons with matched random errors, error decomposition into two kinds, or whether retaining the error improves circuits or steering. The study's recommendation metrics are recorded as findings about reconstruction replacement, not as tests of those claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE interpretability and steering study on recommender transformers. Table 1 reports aggregate reconstruction RMSE, explained variance and L0 across an L1-penalty sweep. It also reports recommendation metrics after replacing activations with reconstructions. That is the standard sparsity–reconstruction trade-off, reported as the study's own hyperparameter selection. The study never asks whether the residual is structured, linearly predictable, pathological relative to random errors, or an artifact of training. It does not cite or engage the dark-matter work. Rising RMSE with stronger L1 (with L0 falling from 821 to 0.5) cannot show that dark matter mostly reflects training rather than model structure. V6 is about the structured residual persisting at matched sparsity, or shrinking with better architectures or objectives, and neither is tested. The dictionary-size statement is aggregate, without numbers, and at a fixed L1. So it cannot speak to V2's per-token predictability or same-context failure.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAEs learn interpretable, largely monosemantic features in sequential recommenders, more interpretable than raw neurons. Steering these features flexibly controls recommendations, and quality degrades at large activation values. Future work could try JumpReLU or TopK SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains classic L1-regularized SAEs on normalized activations from a recommender transformer and evaluates reconstruction replacement and recommendation behavior. It does not use the original study's dark-matter analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: L1 penalty strongly affects reconstruction and recommendation metrics; dictionary size has little effect on reconstruction error from 512 to 8192. The study states it used the first transformer block because it had slightly better interpretability metrics, while other layers gave similar results.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing one layer's output with its SAE reconstruction leaves NDCG/HitRate/Coverage unchanged at low L1. At L1=0.1 (explained variance 0.958), metrics fall slightly (NDCG 0.100 to 0.098). They degrade strongly at L1 ≥ 0.4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommender transformers, the downstream cost of SAE reconstruction replacement scales with the sparsity penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggregate reconstruction RMSE rises with the L1 penalty as L0 falls, at dictionary size 2048.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction error trades off against sparsity via the L1 coefficient (standard trade-off).

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed L1, reconstruction error is reported stable for dictionary sizes 512 to 8192.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed L1, aggregate reconstruction error is insensitive to dictionary size in small recommender transformers.

record.problems: The dark-matter properties in the claim are not directly analyzed. The relevant reconstruction measurements are aggregate rather than per-token, the dictionary-size result is given without numeric values, and the study does not compare reconstruction with matched random errors or report uncertainty for the reconstruction results.
record.rows_left_out: None. All reconstruction RMSE values in Table 1, the dictionary-size reconstruction-error statement in Section 6, and all recommendation metrics in Table 1 are recorded.

untested.parts: No linear prediction of SAE error from input activations.
No per-token error norms, cross-size prediction, or same-context overlap. There is only a qualitative aggregate statement on dictionary size.
No comparison of reconstruction-induced loss with random errors of matched norm.
No decomposition of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
Steering uses the SAE decoder reconstruction, but no comparison is made with versus without the error term.
No comparison of architectures, shrinkage, dead latents or end-to-end training at matched sparsity. There is no analysis of residual structure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is removed. The L1 sweep shows only the expected sparsity–reconstruction trade-off, and dark matter is never examined. The control rows R10–R12 are reference values rather than results. BERT4Rec and Music4All reconstruction numbers are not reported. No uncertainty is given for Table 1.

versions.untested_parts: No linear prediction of SAE error from input activations is measured.
No per-token error norms, cross-size token overlap, or persistence of error across sizes is measured.
The study does not compare model loss under SAE reconstruction with matched random errors.
The study does not separate linear and nonlinear residual components or test further dictionary learning on either.
The study does not compare downstream analyses with the SAE error term retained versus omitted.

It varies the L1 penalty and reports reconstruction error, but does not test shrinkage, dead latents, alternative SAE architectures, end-to-end training, or whether the residual's structure is an artifact rather than a property of the model representation.

reader_labels.reason: Reconstruction RMSE varies with the L1 penalty and is higher at stronger penalties, providing narrow evidence that sparsity settings affect residual magnitude (R1-R8); the study does not show that the residual is mostly a training artifact.
